Building your offer

  • Ask what the candidate leaves behind: unvested stock and this year's bonus. A sign-on bonus or a larger first-year grant is the usual way to cover it.
  • Quote total compensation (base, target bonus and yearly equity value), not base alone. Tech candidates compare offers that way.
  • At a startup, put the vesting schedule, cliff and refresh policy in writing. Candidates discount equity they do not understand.

Building your offer

  • Time the offer around bonus season. Finance candidates who leave before their bonus is paid expect to be made whole.
  • Put the target bonus in the offer letter as a percentage of salary. Finance candidates compare targets, not promises.
  • For controller and CFO hires at private equity-backed companies, explain how the equity pays out at a sale and what the hurdle is.

Building your offer

  • Many support and admin roles have no bonus plan. A spot-award or retention-bonus program is a low-cost way to compete.
  • For HR and operations leaders, equity is the biggest gap between public and private employers. If you cannot offer it, a multi-year cash incentive can stand in.
  • Spell out bonus eligibility in the offer. Candidates for operations roles often assume there is none.

Private equity-backed companies

How PE pay is structured, and why it is different

Private equity-backed companies pay differently from public companies and startups. Cash is steady; the real money is a share of the equity pool that pays out when the investor sells, usually tied to the return the investor makes.

10%of the company is set aside as the management equity pool (median)
23% / 7% / 3%of that pool goes to the CEO, the CFO and each other C-suite leader (medians)
79%of plans with performance vesting measure the investor's return multiple (MOIC)
$604Kaverage total cash for US PE-backed CFOs, up 5% in a year

How the equity pool works

Size

The pool is about 10% of the company. 75% is granted when the investor buys in; 25% is held back for new hires and promotions.

Who gets it

About 15 people at the start, roughly 2% of employees. On a 10% pool, a CFO's 7% share works out to about 0.7% of the company.

What it is

Profits interest units at half of companies, stock options at 30%, restricted shares at 28%. Profits interests now outnumber options.

How it vests and pays out

Time and performance

28% of plans put performance conditions on every award and 43% on some. The usual test is the investor's return multiple (MOIC); some use internal rate of return (IRR) or equity value growth.

Schedule

At PE-backed corporations about 71% of executive grants vest monthly and just over 70% have a one-year cliff; LLCs mostly vest annually.

When it pays

At the sale of the company. Expected payouts for PE-backed CEOs still top $10M at a sale in the base case.

Cash: salary and bonus

CEOs

Average base salary $488K with a target bonus of $295K at PE-backed companies.

CFOs

Average total cash $604K in 2025. When weighing a role, CFOs rank base salary (73%) and equity (69%) far above the annual bonus (35%).

Below the C-suite

Equity is rarer than at public companies of the same size; many companies use a cash long-term bonus for key people outside the equity plan. Grants below the C-suite are usually under 0.01% of the company.

Your own money in

Rollover

32% of companies require some executives to roll over part of their sale proceeds into the new company, typically 20%, for a median of 4 people.

Co-investment

39% offer a voluntary co-investment program, usually with no limit. 84% add no match or discount.

Refresh

Refresh grants to executives at PE-backed LLCs grew from 46% to 73% of the first grant between 2023 and 2025.

Questions to ask in a PE offer

  • Ask what share of the pool the role gets, not just the percentage of the company, and how much of the pool is still unallocated.
  • Ask what return multiple (MOIC) triggers full vesting and what happens to unvested units if the company is sold early.
  • Expect a candidate from a public company to ask for more cash: PE equity pays only when the company is sold.

Public companies

Stock options (incentive or non-qualified). Only about 3% of startup grants are restricted stock units. The standard is four years with a one-year cliff, then monthly vesting.

3Key terms and risks to check

Exercise window after leaving

Most companies give 90 days to buy vested options after you leave. Only 28% of these options get exercised in that window. Ask for an extended window.

Carta, Exercising stock options, 2026-09 ↗
Acceleration on a sale

Double-trigger acceleration means vesting speeds up only if the company is sold and you lose your job. Lawyers call it the sensible middle ground; single-trigger (on the sale alone) rarely makes sense for most employees.

Orrick, Single and double trigger acceleration, 2026-04 ↗
409A price vs. investor price

The 409A price sets the strike price on options. It usually runs 20% to 40% below what investors paid for preferred shares, which have extra rights.

Launchrock, 409A valuation, 2026-05 ↗
Dilution

Each funding round and each pool top-up shrinks your percentage. Ask for the fully diluted share count and how many shares are outstanding.

Carta, 2026 Founder Ownership Report, 2026-03 ↗
The cliff

Leave before the first year and you keep nothing. After the cliff, 1/48 of the grant vests each month on a standard schedule.

Carta, Vesting: schedules, cliffs and acceleration, 2026-07 ↗

Target bonusThe bonus paid for hitting plan, shown as a share of salary. Actual payouts move with results.
Equity and long-term incentiveStock, options or cash that vests over several years. It rewards staying and growing company value.
Share of the companyAt private companies equity is quoted as a percentage of ownership. It pays out only at a sale or public offering.

  • Current data only. Every figure was published or collected in 2026. The one exception is the U.S. Dept. of Labor wage survey, whose latest release covers May 2025.
  • U.S. Dept. of Labor (BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2025): New York-Newark-Jersey City metro, plus New Jersey and Connecticut statewide.
  • Job postings with posted salary ranges in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, posted in the last six months (May 10 to November 10, 2026), from Google Jobs, company career sites and job boards.
  • Salary sites: Glassdoor, PayScale, Salary.com, ZipRecruiter, Built In, Comparably and Levels.fyi, New York figures, collected November 2026.
  • Bonus and long-term incentives: SEC proxy filings of public companies headquartered in the New York area, and published executive pay surveys.

How the numbers are set

  • Vaco by Highspring adjustment. Pay figures are adjusted using Vaco by Highspring’s recruiting experience in the New York, New Jersey and Connecticut market.
  • Vaco recommended offer (in each role card and the hiring advisor): a range from the typical figure up to about the 65th percentile (the typical figure plus 60% of the way to the upper end). Offers toward the top of the range win strong candidates in a competitive search. It is Vaco’s advice, not a market average.
  • Vaco by Highspring internal data counts twice and is never dropped as an outlier.
  • Client services roles (added November 2026). Client Service Associate, Client Service Manager and Director of Client Services use 2026 New York figures from PayScale and 2026 New York job postings in financial services.
  • Yearly bonus and total pay. The bonus is how far total pay runs above base salary on Glassdoor and PayScale for the same role. Because those totals can include stock, the bonus is capped at typical 2026 bonus targets: 10% of base for early-career roles, 15% for individual and manager roles, 25% for directors. Executive bonuses are not capped. Stock is shown separately.
  • Security leadership recheck (November 2026). Director of Information Security, VP of Information Security and Chief Information Security Officer add 2026 New York figures from Salary.com, PayScale and Orbyt Salary Explorer to the job postings, Dept. of Labor and Glassdoor data. The career-ladder rule applies, so pay rises from Manager to Director to VP to CISO.
  • Each source counts once, except Vaco internal data. The typical salary is the middle of the sources’ typical figures; the range is the middle of their low and high figures (25th and 75th percentiles where published).
  • Accounting and finance titles: Early career is the staff or analyst title, Experienced is the senior title (the 4 to 6 year job), Senior is the upper end of the senior title.
  • Outlier rule: any source figure more than 15% below or 35% above the middle of all sources for that role is left out, so one site that reads far off the rest cannot pull a role down or up.
  • Where a senior title was combined into its base role, the Experienced figure sits between the two titles, because senior is a matter of years, not a different job.
  • Job postings: the middle of posted low and high ends, and of the midpoints. Duplicates, hourly and contract roles, and postings older than six months are excluded.
  • Financial Services figures use postings from banks, insurers, investment firms and private equity, plus Vaco internal data. Accounting & Finance figures exclude those employers.
  • New Jersey and Connecticut are compared with New York source by source: each source's state figure is set against the same source's New York figure for that role, and the typical gap is applied to the New York pay. Where a role has fewer than two matching sources, the state's typical gap to New York is used. A state is shown above New York only when the matching sources support it.
  • Industry views use real pay data. Where a role has no figure of its own for an industry (too few postings of its own), it is worked out from how that industry pays for roles in the same skill area, or else for all roles.
  • Base annual salary unless stated. Bonus and equity figures are shown separately, with their sources.
